questions.q: Safety in operations is whose responsibility?
options: Line responsibility — every staff member owns the safety of their own task
questions.explain: Safety is line responsibility: each person owns their task's safety; supervisors verify, they do not merely trust.

questions.q: What is the supervisor's safety role?
options: To verify that work is done safely — not merely trust that it was
questions.explain: Supervisors verify. Trust without verification is how unsafe habits grow unnoticed.

questions.q: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is mandatory where?
options: In depots, on tracks and in workshops, as prescribed
questions.explain: Helmets, gloves, hi-vis and other Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) as prescribed are compulsory in depots, tracks and workshops.

questions.q: Which discipline rule applies to alcohol and drugs on duty?
options: No duty under alcohol/drugs — breath-analyser checks are standard
questions.explain: Zero tolerance: breath-analyser checks are a standard part of railway discipline.

questions.q: Using a mobile phone in a way that distracts from safety duty is:
options: Prohibited — no mobile distraction on safety duty
questions.explain: A distracted operator is a failed barrier. Mobile distraction on safety duty is a discipline offence.

questions.q: 'Normalisation of deviance' means:
options: Repeated small shortcuts gradually becoming accepted as normal — a known cause of accidents
Following rules more strictly over time
questions.explain: When shortcuts stop shocking anyone, the accident is already on its way — that drift is normalisation of deviance.

questions.q: A staff member feels too fatigued to perform safety duty safely. Reporting this is:
options: A protected act — prescribed rest and fitness for duty are safety requirements
questions.explain: Fatigue is a hazard. Reporting unfitness is protected — the system wants the report, not a tired operator.

questions.q: Prescribed rest for operational staff exists because:
options: Fatigue degrades attention and decision-making, raising accident risk
questions.explain: Rest is a safety control, not a perk — tired staff miss signals, messages and hazards.

questions.q: Safety-critical communication requires which elements?
options: Identification, a clear message, read-back and confirmation
questions.explain: Say who you are, say it clearly, hear it repeated back, confirm it — that is safety-critical communication.

questions.q: Read-back in safety-critical communication means:
options: The receiver repeats the message back so the sender can confirm it was heard correctly
questions.explain: Read-back catches hearing errors before they become movement errors — the telephone game played honestly.

questions.q: Why are casual tone and nicknames unacceptable in safety-critical communication?
options: They create ambiguity about who is speaking and what is instructed
questions.explain: Standard, identified, unambiguous speech is itself a safety barrier.

questions.q: Operational discipline includes which of these?
options: Following rules, taking no shortcuts, keeping unauthorised persons out of cab/control areas, and fitness for duty
questions.explain: Discipline is behaviour when nobody is watching — rules followed, shortcuts refused, areas kept secure, staff fit.

questions.q: Scenario: A colleague suggests skipping a check 'because we always do and nothing happens'. This thinking is:
options: Normalisation of deviance — the shortcut must be refused and the full procedure followed
questions.explain: 'Nothing happened last time' is the most dangerous sentence in operations — refuse the shortcut.

questions.q: Scenario: You are called for safety duty but have had almost no sleep. The correct action is:
options: Report yourself unfit as per rules — reporting unfitness is protected
Take duty and drink tea to stay awake
Take duty and avoid telling anyone
Ask a passenger to keep you awake
questions.explain: An unfit operator is a hazard to hundreds. Report it; the system protects that honesty.

questions.q: Who is responsible for the safety of a task — the worker or the supervisor?
options: Both: the worker owns the safety of the task; the supervisor verifies it is done safely
questions.explain: Ownership sits with the doer, verification with the supervisor — both layers are required.

questions.q: A breath-analyser check before safety duty is best understood as:
options: A standard fitness-for-duty control, applied routinely
A formality that can be skipped
questions.explain: Routine checks keep the zero-alcohol rule real; they are a control, not an accusation.

questions.q: What should a receiver do if a safety-critical message is unclear?
options: Ask for it to be repeated/rephrased and confirm by read-back before acting
Act on the most likely meaning
questions.explain: Unclear message = no action until it is clear and read back. Guessing is not a procedure.

questions.q: Why must unauthorised persons be kept out of cabs and control areas?
options: They can distract staff and interfere with safety-critical work
questions.explain: Cab and control areas are safety workplaces — access is restricted to authorised staff only.

questions.q: Which habit best shows operational discipline?
options: Following the laid-down procedure fully, even when a shortcut would save time and nobody is watching
Depending on memory instead of procedure
questions.explain: Discipline is what you do unsupervised — the full procedure, every time.

questions.q: Fatigue, distraction and shortcuts are grouped together in the book as:
options: Human-factor threats to safety that discipline and rostering must control
questions.explain: Alcohol, mobiles, fatigue and shortcuts all attack the human barrier — discipline is the counter-control.

questions.q: If an Operations Control Centre (OCC) instruction is received, the receiver must:
options: Identify themselves, listen, read back the instruction and confirm before executing
questions.explain: Identify — listen — read back — confirm — then execute. Skipping read-back skips the error check.

questions.q: A staff member notices a supervisor repeatedly ignoring a safety procedure. The right course is:
options: Report it through the proper channel — safety responsibility applies at every level
Discuss it only in the canteen
questions.explain: No rank exempts anyone from safety rules; reporting through the proper channel is the protected route.

questions.q: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) protects best when:
options: It is carried in the hand
It is worn only for photographs
It is worn as prescribed, as the last line of defence behind procedure and protection
questions.explain: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is mandatory but it is the last line — possession, isolation and procedure come before it.

questions.q: What is the link between discipline and safety-critical communication?
options: Disciplined communication — standard format, identification, read-back — is part of operational discipline
questions.explain: How you speak on duty is discipline: standard, identified, read back and confirmed.

questions.q: The statement 'supervisors verify, they do not merely trust' teaches that:
options: Supervisors should do all work themselves
Verification is an active safety duty of supervision, not a paper exercise
Verification is optional for experienced staff
questions.explain: A supervisor's signature should mean 'I checked', not 'I assumed' — that is the safety culture the exam tests.

questions.q: Safety-critical communication must use standard phraseology and avoid slang or private shortcuts mainly because:
options: Standard words have one agreed meaning for every sender and receiver, while slang and shortcuts can be understood differently under stress
questions.explain: In an emergency there is no time to decode personal styles. Standard phraseology is a shared code: the same words, the same meaning, for a driver, a station controller and Operations Control Centre (OCC) alike.

questions.q: The phonetic alphabet (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie…) is used in radio communication to:
options: Distinguish similar-sounding letters and numbers (like B/D or 5/9) so identifiers, train numbers and locations are copied exactly
questions.explain: On a noisy radio channel, 'B' and 'D' sound alike but 'Bravo' and 'Delta' never do. The phonetic alphabet removes letter-confusion from safety-critical identifiers.

questions.q: A staff member reports for safety-critical duty under the influence of alcohol. In railway discipline this is treated as:
options: A serious offence — the person must be removed from safety duty and dealt with under disciplinary rules, because impaired staff endanger everyone
questions.explain: Alcohol slows reaction and judgement exactly in the faculties safety duty depends on. 'Feeling fine' is not a test — reporting under influence is itself a grave breach of safety discipline.

questions.q: 'Stop-work authority' in a safety culture means:
options: Only the senior-most officer may stop work
Any staff member who sees an imminent danger has the authority — and the duty — to stop the work or movement immediately and report it
Work stops only at shift end
questions.explain: Danger does not wait for hierarchy. Empowering the person who actually sees the hazard to stop the job is one of the strongest real-world safety barriers, and good organisations protect staff who use it in good faith.

questions.q: A safety-critical shift handover is complete only when:
options: The outgoing staff member leaves on time
Defects, restrictions, pending instructions and abnormal conditions are handed over verbally AND recorded in the log, and the incoming staff member has understood and accepted them
The register is signed without reading
Only the train positions are mentioned
questions.explain: Most handovers fail silently — something known to one shift never reaches the next. Verbal briefing plus a written log plus confirmed understanding closes all three gaps.
